dovish.title: September Payrolls Cracked: +29k vs ~90k; Prior Months Revised 60k Lower
dovish.summary: The labor market cracked in September: payrolls +29k against a ~90k street, unemployment up to 4.2%, July-August revised a combined 60k lower, and wages up only 0.1% m/m — the October hike debate has flipped toward hold.
dovish.source: BLS Employment Situation, September 2026 (released Oct 2 08:30 ET; official series via the BLS public API — the bls.gov release page returned HTTP 403 this round; wire mirror bound)

data.unit: thousand jobs, m/m change, seasonally adjusted (September 2026)

dovish.reason: The September Employment Situation (released Oct 2, 08:30 ET) is the fissure: payrolls +29k against a ~90k street, with July revised down 31k to -10k and August down 29k to +133k — a combined -60k revision that raises the bar for calling this noise. Unemployment rose to 4.2% on rising participation (61.8%); average hourly earnings slowed to +0.1% m/m (3.0% y/y). Health care (+17k) and construction (+11k) carried what little job creation there was. For the Fed's reaction function this is the strongest dovish entry since the Sep 16 hike: it removes the labor-market argument for another hike at Oct 28. Weight 2.0 — the month's flagship release, a ~61k headline miss with negative net revisions; the card moved from the hawkish side per the refresh rule because the reading reversed. Market validation: ZN=F +0.25% across the release window; CAD futures +0.11%.

decision_brief.summary: A weekend snapshot with nothing new to price: markets have been shut since Friday 16:00 and no US or Canadian release has landed, so every figure here is Friday's, re-confirmed from freshly captured bytes. The standing picture: September payrolls cracked (+29k against a ~90k street; unemployment 4.2%; July-August revised a combined 60k lower), both central banks are on hold (Fed 3.75-4.00% into Oct 27-28; BoC 2.25% into Oct 28), and the rope leans dovish (net -1.0) against an intact-but-small hawkish column (core PCE 3.0% y/y; ISM prices-paid 77.9; Michigan 1-year expectations 4.6%). What can be verified still sits at policy: ZQV26's last bar (96.120) implies a 3.88% October monthly (30-day) average EFFR - the pre-decision regime, +0.5 bp over the range midpoint - and CRAU26 quotes (bid 97.6525 / ask 97.655; no executed print in this weekend capture) around a 2.346% quarterly average CORRA across the Oct 28 and Dec 9 decisions. CME FedWatch is dark again (HTTP 403), so no single-meeting distribution exists in this snapshot and none is invented. The week decides whether the dovish turn extends or the inflation counterweight returns: ISM services Monday, minutes Wednesday, claims Thursday, Canada LFS and Michigan Friday. With nothing dislocated, there is still no trade.

The contract averages almost the whole month before the Oct 28 decision, so it measures October's starting regime, not the meeting's outcome. Separately, media coverage (AlphaPilot, Oct 1, citing CME FedWatch) reported market-implied odds of another hike on Oct 28 above 70% - that figure predates Friday's payrolls print, which removed its labor argument, and this environment cannot verify it (direct FedWatch requests return HTTP 403); stale context, not data. fed.stance: Hold at 3.75-4.00% into Oct 27-28 - Friday's payroll crack is still the last hard data; no verifiable meeting distribution
fed.rationale: The Sep 16 FOMC raised the target range 25 bp to 3.75-4.00%. The last hard data point remains Friday's September Employment Situation: +29k vs a ~90k street, unemployment 4.2%, and a combined -60k revision to July-August - the labor argument for another hike is gone, and wages (+0.1% m/m, 3.0% y/y) softened too. The counterweight is inflation (core PCE 3.0% y/y; ISM prices-paid 77.9; Michigan 1-year expectations 4.6%). FedWatch returned HTTP 403 again this weekend, so no single-meeting distribution exists; ZQV26's last bar is 96.120 (3.88% October average, +0.5 bp over the range midpoint) - the pre-decision regime, not the meeting. Net: hold is the strong base case, and this week's confirmation sequence decides whether the next debate is the timing of an easing bias.
